problem.text: Let ε < 1/2 be a positive real number and let U_ε denote the set of real numbers that differ from their nearest integer by at most ε. Prove that there exists a positive integer m such that for any real number x, the sets {x, 2x, 3x, …, mx} and U_ε have at least one element in common.

spans.reason: Quantifier order: m is chosen before x and may depend only on ε. The bound must be uniform in x, which kills any argument that picks m after seeing x.

spans.text: differ from their nearest integer by at most ε
spans.reason: This is the distance to the nearest integer, ‖t‖ ≤ ε. U_ε is periodic with period 1, so the whole problem lives on the circle ℝ/ℤ, where it is an arc of length 2ε around 0.
Consecutive multiples of one number: their fractional parts are a constant-step walk on the circle, and the difference of two of them is again a multiple of x.
Only there to keep U_ε from being all of ℝ; it does not drive the argument.

definitions.meaning_latex: \lVert t \rVert = \min_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \lvert t - n \rvert, \text{ the distance from } t \text{ to the nearest integer}
U_\varepsilon = \{ t \in \mathbb{R} : \lVert t \rVert \le \varepsilon \}, \text{ an arc of length } 2\varepsilon \text{ around } 0 \text{ on } \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}

goal.asked: A positive integer m, depending on ε only, such that some multiple kx with 1 ≤ k ≤ m is within ε of an integer, for every real x.
goal.answer_form: A construction of m from ε plus a proof.
goal.final_line_would_say: Hence some kx with 1 ≤ k ≤ m satisfies ‖kx‖ ≤ ε.

informal_cues.bearing: 'Any real' includes irrational x, where the multiples never repeat; nothing periodic can be assumed, so the argument must be a count, not a cycle.
ε < 1/2 only stops U_ε from being everything; no step of the proof uses more of it.

underneath.really_is: an arc of length 2ε around 0 on the circle ℝ/ℤ
underneath.implies: 'kx ∈ U_ε' is the one-line statement ‖kx‖ ≤ ε

underneath.really_is: m points on the circle, plus the point 0 for free
underneath.implies: m + 1 points against ⌈1/ε⌉ arcs of length at most ε forces two points into one arc

underneath.really_is: jx − ix = (j−i)x, a multiple with a smaller index
underneath.implies: two walk points landing close together hands us one multiple close to an integer

deeper_properties: $\lVert a - b \rVert \le \lvert \{a\} - \{b\} \rvert$: if two fractional parts are within ε of each other, their difference is within ε of an integer.
Cutting the circle into $\lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil$ arcs of length at most ε and placing the m + 1 points 0, x, …, mx collides two of them whenever $m \ge \lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil$.
The count never looks at x, which is exactly the uniformity the quantifier order demands: $m = \lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil$ works for every x at once.

simplification.instance: Take ε = 1/4. Place the points 0, x, 2x, 3x, 4x on the circle.
simplification.what_to_try: Split the circle into four arcs of length 1/4 and count points against arcs.
simplification.notice_prompt: Two of five points share an arc, so their difference is a multiple of x within 1/4 of an integer. How many points do you need for a general ε, and does the count depend on x at all?

candidates.name: Pigeonhole on fractional parts of 0, x, …, mx (Dirichlet's approximation)
candidates.from_first_principles: The bound must be uniform in x, so count instead of approximating: cut the circle into $\lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil$ arcs of length at most ε and place the m + 1 points 0, x, …, mx with $m = \lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil$. Two points ix and jx share an arc, so $\lVert (j-i)x \rVert \le \varepsilon$ with $1 \le j - i \le m$.
candidates.why: Produces m from ε alone and uses every quantifier exactly as written.

candidates.name: Equidistribution of {kx} for irrational x
candidates.from_first_principles: For irrational x the fractional parts of the multiples are dense, so some kx lands in the arc.
candidates.why: True, but gives no uniform m and says nothing about rational x.

candidates.name: Case split rational / irrational
candidates.from_first_principles: Rational x = p/q is finished by k = q, since qx is an integer; treat irrational x separately.
candidates.why: The rational case is easy but the irrational case needs the pigeonhole anyway, so the split buys nothing.

candidates.name: Continued fractions
candidates.from_first_principles: The convergents of x give the best rational approximations, hence small ‖qx‖.
candidates.why: Gives best approximations; far more than needed.

method.chosen: Pigeonhole with m = ⌈1/ε⌉: two of the points 0, x, …, mx share an arc of length at most ε, so their difference kx satisfies ‖kx‖ ≤ ε with 1 ≤ k ≤ m.
